content: Maternal health care is a comprehensive concept that includes preconception, prenatal, and postnatal care. Preconception care aims to promote health, conduct screenings, and provide interventions for women of reproductive age to minimize risk factors that could negatively impact future pregnancies. Prenatal care involves the thorough medical attention women receive and provide for themselves throughout pregnancy. Women who initiate prenatal care early in their pregnancies tend to experience better birth outcomes compared to those who receive little or no care during pregnancy. Postnatal care addresses recovery from childbirth, concerns about newborn care, nutrition, breastfeeding, and family planning. A significant issue is that most women lack access to essential healthcare and sexual health education services. In many developing countries, complications arising from pregnancy and childbirth, particularly during the preconception and prenatal stages, are the leading causes of death among women of reproductive age. Tragically, more than one woman dies every minute from such causes, amounting to approximately 585,000 deaths annually, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Less than 1% of these deaths occur in developed countries, highlighting that these fatalities are largely preventable with adequate resources and services. Any woman can experience sudden and unexpected complications during pregnancy, childbirth, or the postpartum period. While high-quality, accessible healthcare has made maternal deaths rare in developed nations, these complications often prove fatal in developing regions. Consequently, maternal mortality rates in developing countries are over 100 times higher than in developed nations. Access to emergency obstetric care, which is critical for saving lives, is not prioritized in many of these regions. Barriers preventing women in developing countries from accessing necessary healthcare include long distances to health facilities, high costs (including direct fees, transportation, medications, and supplies), competing demands on their time, and a lack of decision-making power within their families. Additionally, the poor quality of healthcare services, including mistreatment by providers, discourages some women from seeking care. According to the 2004 World Health Report, poor maternal health conditions are the fourth leading cause of death among women, following HIV/AIDS, malaria, and tuberculosis. Alarmingly, 99% of these deaths occur in low-income countries. While the risk of dying from pregnancy or childbirth in developed nations is 1 in 4,000, women in Sub-Saharan Africa face a 1 in 16 chance of dying. Maternal health issues also account for nearly 20% of the total disease burden for women in developing countries. Furthermore, almost 50% of births in these regions occur without the assistance of a skilled attendant, with the proportion being even higher in South Asia. Providing basic family planning, maternal, and neonatal healthcare to women in developing countries could be achieved with an investment of just $3 per person annually. Many non-profit organizations are working to educate the public and improve access to emergency obstetric care for mothers in these regions. Essential services include routine maternal care for all pregnancies, skilled attendants (such as midwives or doctors) at births, emergency treatment for complications during pregnancy, delivery, and postpartum, postpartum family planning, basic neonatal care, and community education on the importance of maternal health care. Empowering women to make healthcare decisions and seek medical attention is also critical. By region, there are notable trends in maternal health improvement. Regions that have met the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) for maternal health include Sub-Saharan Africa, Southeastern Asia, Southern Asia, and Oceania. Regions making slow progress include Northern Africa, Western Asia, and Latin America and the Caribbean. Regions showing no or negative progress include Eastern Asia and Europe (specifically the Commonwealth of Independent States). Despite significant advancements in maternal health over the past century, the last decade has seen a slow rate of improvement in maternal mortality and morbidity, particularly in Latin America and the Caribbean. Currently, only about 17% of countries are on track to meet the MDGs for maternal health.
